sources.title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
sources.note: Full transcript plus README. Dex co-hosts; first ~20 min is Dex on workflow and models, then the layered factory model. Vaibhav's BAML factory and code mode demo not carded except where Dex endorses.

sources.title: AI That Works: Code Mode for Extensible Software
sources.note: Full transcript. Dex is absent (Vaibhav hosts, Kyle Mistele guest). Only Kyle's own ideas carded; the BAML type-checking demo is Vaibhav's and was not carded.

sources.title: AI That Works: Software Factories: Hands on with Real Builders
sources.note: Full transcript plus README. Guests Tyler Brown and Cole Murray; carded only what Dex argues or explicitly endorses.

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: queuing up like 15 prompts to let them just argue it out overnight
cards.claim: Dex queues about 15 prompts overnight (implement, review, have the Codex CLI review, compact, repeat) so two models argue a feature out, then does human polish in the morning.
cards.evidence_detail: His own current workflow for large features; cheap in human time because of subscriptions; no numbers on quality.
cards.landing: Workflow-tool script: implement then cross-model review then compact loop, saved as a reusable workflow
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'm not asking anyone to review a twenty K line PR
cards.claim: A large prototype 'slop PR' is used as a spec to learn what is wanted, then the model re-plans it into separate 1-3k line PRs with migrations placed deliberately; about 90% of work is small enough to ship in one pass.
cards.evidence_detail: First five PRs shipped about one a day; PR 5 got a reviewer architecture objection; the 90% figure is an estimate.
cards.landing: Phase routine: rule for splitting oversized changes into digestible PRs; PR-size limit in reviewer checklist
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I basically like, here's a transcript of a thing
cards.claim: Dex does not let models write long text: he has the model write two or three sentences at a time, edits them, and has it continue in the same session so it picks up tone, optionally backed by a doc of anti-patterns.
cards.evidence_detail: His writing process; says three pages of model output is unreadable to him so he works in small increments.
cards.landing: Reviewer and closing-message format: small increments for owner-facing prose; one-page owner view
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're just compensating for the fact that you're using a worse model
cards.claim: Dex relays Peter Steinberger's October 2025 view that the research-up-front scaffolding was compensation for a weaker model, and that a model which reads longer on its own makes it unnecessary.
cards.evidence_detail: Second-hand conversation recollection; Dex notes Codex then was not better than Opus; he himself now does 90-95% of features with Codex.
cards.landing: Re-check each phase-routine step for whether it compensates for a weaker model; candidate for CLAUDE.md trim
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: ninety or ninety five percent of the features I write are written with
cards.claim: Dex routes by task type: the Codex-family model writes 90-95% of features and costs most; Opus/Fable models are kept for generic knowledge work and UI, invoked as a sub-agent or a fresh session when the UI output is poor.
cards.evidence_detail: Shown on a cost-by-model usage screen; no quality numbers.
cards.landing: Model routing per phase or agent: choose implementer vs UI/reviewer model; workflow script model parameter
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: HTML mockups, they don't have to be faithful
cards.claim: Before a big build, Dex does research and product-outline back and forth with the model and produces HTML interaction mocks, which only need to convey direction, as the spec for an overnight implementation.
cards.evidence_detail: Demonstrated on a PRD canvas; feature took a day or two for spec plus a day for mocks, then PR a day.
cards.landing: Phase 0 / planning step: low-fidelity mocks as a plan artifact for UI-bearing phases
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you are going to want to own this
cards.claim: Dex's thesis is that outside toy apps you will want to own the dev environment (language runtimes, external testing, shared services) because vendor sandboxes add friction such as poking holes to shared services and odd kernels.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued from experience with customers having 50+ shared services and 100 repos; no data.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (infrastructure: FixFlow dev env is local plus Railway)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you could pick cattle, but then you're bulk cloning all the repos
cards.claim: Dex treats pets (a long-lived box) as a fine starting point until you have thousands of workflows, and says multi-repo work needs one canonical coordination place with a model told where the other repos are, no submodules or symlinks required.
cards.evidence_detail: Runs a pet server himself; multi-repo template referenced as in use at HumanLayer's customers.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (FixFlow is one monorepo); relevant only if repos are split
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: neither of these support hooks
cards.claim: Dex says the standard harness-to-UI protocols (ACP, AG-UI) lack hooks, the lifecycle events a control plane needs, and that Claude Code, Codex, Pi and OpenCode implement hooks incompatibly; HumanLayer uses hooks.
cards.evidence_detail: Observation about protocol coverage; no data.
cards.landing: Hooks (previously skipped by the harness review): hooks are the lifecycle mechanism a control plane uses to observe compliance
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's like composition over inheritance, right?
cards.claim: Dex argues for open interfaces so a team can buy or build any layer (compute, dev environment, harness, orchestration) without buying everything below it.
cards.evidence_detail: Design principle stated; HumanLayer positioned as swappable harness with orchestration.
cards.landing: Keep harness-specific config (hooks, skills) separable from workflow logic so scripts are portable
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: don't wrap interfaces with other interfaces or don't wrap APIs with other APIs
cards.claim: Dex recalls a team rule from an earlier job: do not wrap an official SDK in your own thin client, call it directly at each call site.
cards.evidence_detail: Remembered rule from Sprout, offered as design heuristic.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (code-design guidance; could be a CLAUDE.md or lint note)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: how do you incorporate that into your your outer harness basically?
cards.claim: Dex lists 'compounding engineering' as a control-plane function: repeated corrections by many engineers to the agent should flow back into the outer harness as shared memory.
cards.evidence_detail: References an episode a month earlier; no mechanism given here.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store design for verified diagnoses; skill or CLAUDE.md updates from recurring corrections
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: vibable zones and they have no vibe zones
cards.claim: Dex endorses splitting a codebase into no-vibe zones (functional core, strict interfaces) where the factory builds user-reported bugs and vibable zones where looser code is allowed, including user-deployed extensions.
cards.evidence_detail: Described as a pattern 'many people have talked about'; no example from his code.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md invariants already name no-touch areas (money, lifecycle, dispatcher); could be turned into explicit zones with differing verification levels
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: If it gets if it if it de dupes half of the things, then you've saved yourself
cards.claim: Dex says an imperfect automated stage (deduping half of issues) is still worth it, and that a repro-first pipeline only works for issues with clear code repros while hard-to-reproduce ones need an agent to try to create one.
cards.evidence_detail: Reaction to Vaibhav's pipeline; no measurements.
cards.landing: Verification design: repro-first gate before a fix register item is accepted
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: other
cards.quote: That's a hard coded while loop
cards.claim: Vaibhav's factory drives a PR to merge with a hard-coded while loop that fixes bot review comments until mergeable or three iterations, then hands to a human; Dex restates it as 'or until three iterations get hit'.
cards.evidence_detail: Boundary's in-house practice; Dex restates but does not add his own evidence.
cards.landing: Workflow script: bounded fix loop with max iterations then human escalation
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: This is David Crosshaw's thing of like software should be extensible.
cards.claim: Dex endorses letting users or agents write code against an extension interface instead of building a visual integration manager, and notes Pi and OpenCode already work this way (agent writes code that live-reloads).
cards.evidence_detail: Cites David Crawshaw and Reese's Executor (config by dropping TypeScript files); no demo from HumanLayer.
cards.landing: Saved workflow library as code files in the repo rather than per-task scripts
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: giving the agents a slash bro skill
cards.claim: Dex and Kyle joked about giving agents a skill they can invoke to tell the human their message was unclear; Vaibhav says unclear human instructions are a major source of context problems.
cards.evidence_detail: Joke with a half-serious point; no implementation.
cards.landing: A skill: agent challenges an ambiguous owner instruction before starting a phase
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the dev environment is actually part of the outer harness
cards.claim: Dex floats that the dev environment is part of the outer harness rather than under it; Vaibhav disagrees and puts identity provisioning in the dev environment layer.
cards.evidence_detail: Brief semantic aside, left unresolved.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Software Factory Design Patterns
cards.author: other
cards.quote: much harder than getting a system that's 95% automatic
cards.claim: Vaibhav advises aiming for a 95% automatic factory that escalates the rest to humans rather than a fully automatic one; Dex agrees in passing.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as a common mistake; no data.
cards.landing: Escalation rules in phase routine: define which failures go to the owner instead of retrying
cards.inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 — AI That Works #71 Software Factory Design Patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can outsource the thinking, but you can't outsource the understanding.
cards.claim: Dex says the factory must stream agent-to-human understanding, because once you stop understanding what is being built you end up hoping the agents solve it; maintaining understanding maintains control.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites Jake at Netflix and a Karpathy reply; stated as principle.
cards.landing: One-page owner view and six-question closing message: design for owner understanding, not just completeness
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: A genetic back well, I got that from Jeff Huntley.
cards.claim: Dex agrees with Tyler that verifiers are the top priority (code review is whatever you cannot verify) and links this to backpressure, which he credits to Geoff Huntley.
cards.evidence_detail: Tyler's claim, Dex affirms and links to earlier backpressure episodes.
cards.landing: Backpressure scripts and verifiers: give agents machine-checkable verifiers so review is only what cannot be verified
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: what where did humans have to step in step in
cards.claim: Dex summarises and endorses Tyler's weekly post-mortem loop: record where humans had to step in, file GitHub issues, and each week add one thing to the factory so humans are not needed there next time.
cards.evidence_detail: Tyler's two-person company reports ARR growth from about 270K to under 400K in three months; causal link to the loop is unproven.
cards.landing: Decisions journal and closing message: turn each human intervention into a harness change; weekly register of misses
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: all work in progress is debt
cards.claim: Dex says process engineering means finding and elevating the slowest bottleneck and not stuffing more work into the top of the funnel, because all work in progress is debt.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing principle; no data.
cards.landing: Phase routine: one phase per session already; add WIP limit on open draft PRs awaiting review
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: pair programming now is as important as ever
cards.claim: Dex says agentic coding is asynchronous so solo people drift (check Twitter, start more sessions), whereas pairing keeps you on track and cross-pollinates tips; pairing the agent-fluent with the newcomer teaches the process.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal observation; Vaibhav says Dex taught him in an eight-hour pairing session.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (human process, owner and agent)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we are forced to put all of outsource the learning from the people
cards.claim: Dex says that because non-technical contributors will not learn the dangers themselves, the learning must be moved into the factory (guardrails, skills, prompts, linters), which should evolve after each attempt rather than gate who may contribute.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued in discussion with Cole Murray; no data.
cards.landing: Guardrails as code (lint, import contracts, skills) rather than prose in CLAUDE.md
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: He literally mocked out all of work OS in our app.
cards.claim: Dex endorses re-architecting the app so an agent can run it with as few upstream dependencies as possible (e.g. mocking the login provider) so the factory can test without real credentials.
cards.evidence_detail: One contractor's 3am workaround; also Cole says OAuth login is a standard blocker.
cards.landing: Verifier environment: seeded local login and test credentials for agents; fits FixFlow's local-dev test-credential rules
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every hour you clone every repo onto a base image
cards.claim: Dex describes the pattern of re-baking a base image hourly with all repos cloned so on-demand sessions boot fast and only need a git pull, noting that slow start (five minutes) kills Slack-triggered use.
cards.evidence_detail: Reports that some customers do this and it 'seems to be working okay'.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (infrastructure)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: what feeds work into the factory?
cards.claim: Dex asks what feeds the factory and favours automating intake of work (support exhaust, session recordings, Sentry) so you do not have to sit in Slack; Tyler's orchestrator chat triages a day's notes into tickets with sub-issues and root-cause evidence.
cards.evidence_detail: Tyler's demo: bug report to four Linear sub-tickets with Sentry and PostHog context; Dex asks, does not claim results.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (FixFlow register is owner-curated)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: incremental steps you can take to get there
cards.claim: Dex says adopting AI-native working in a big org must be incremental because doing it in one go is chaos.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as principle in response to Vaibhav; no data.
cards.landing: Phase plan: pilot P1 cold-resume trial before wider routine adoption
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Hands on with Real Builders
cards.author: other
cards.quote: you need a better harness and you need more sort of checks and balances
cards.claim: Tyler Brown claims that as models get more capable the harness and checks matter more, so a three-hour run does not return something to throw away; Dex does not dispute it.
cards.evidence_detail: Tyler's experience running a two-person company; no data.
cards.landing: Verifier and gate strength scaled to model autonomy; relates to hooks and pre-commit gate decisions
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #73

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Code Mode for Extensible Software
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: The agent already knows how to do all these things, just give it the bash tool
cards.claim: Kyle says bash is the simplest code mode, and harnesses are collapsing separate list/grep/glob tools into one shell because the agent composes known Unix tools in one round trip.
cards.evidence_detail: Observation about Claude Code and Pi; no measurements.
cards.landing: Custom agent and skill design: prefer a shell script the agent calls over many narrow tools
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #72

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Code Mode for Extensible Software
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: now there's 60 tools in your context window
cards.claim: Kyle says tool definitions for many MCP servers fill the context window, and code mode over SDK stubs gives dynamic tool discovery and keeps multi-step intermediate output out of context.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoned example (60 tools); no measured token counts.
cards.landing: Context budget: keep MCP and tool lists minimal; load tools on demand
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #72

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Code Mode for Extensible Software
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: code mode is not super in distribution for the models yet
cards.claim: Kyle warns code mode should not be the default because models are not yet trained on it; use it only for shaped problems (many tools needing discovery, composition, in-distribution SDKs, or data structures like CRDTs).
cards.evidence_detail: His judgment from building it; the CRDT editing case is the one worked example.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (tool design guidance)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #72

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Code Mode for Extensible Software
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: design the errors for the agent to be able to figure out what went wrong
cards.claim: Kyle says error design is a major part of building agent code execution: return the error plus captured console output so the agent can see program state and retry, since raw runtime errors are often cryptic.
cards.evidence_detail: From his CRDT implementation with injected console API.
cards.landing: Backpressure scripts: verifier output shaped for the agent (error plus state), not raw logs
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #72

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Code Mode for Extensible Software
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: Letting untrusted code touch an object prototype is incredibly evil.
cards.claim: Kyle says for a multi-tenant backend, agent-written code runs in a WASM QuickJS sandbox with only injected user-scoped bindings; and credentials should be injected by a network proxy outside the sandbox, never visible to the agent.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes his own implementation; the proxy pattern is what 'a lot of folks' do for background agents.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (FixFlow has no agent-code execution; credential-proxy idea relevant to secrets in agent sessions)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #72

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Code Mode for Extensible Software
cards.author: Kyle
cards.quote: execute tools at the speed of code
cards.claim: Kyle says editing a live shared document through ten model round trips risks the document changing under the edit, so a single generated code string should apply atomically; he also notes the task needs a reasonably smart model, not a fast one.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoning from his CRDT build; Vaibhav adds the roughly 300-400 ms per hop figure.
cards.landing: Effort/model routing: cheap fast models are wrong for complex multi-step operations on large structures
cards.inventory_ref: (B) September 2026 — AI That Works #72

gaps: Episode 2 (Code Mode, 2026-09-01) has no Dex; cards are Kyle's only. Vaibhav's BAML compile-time type checking and sandbox demo were not carded.
Transcripts are auto-captions with no speaker labels beyond handles; the first 20 minutes of episode 1 mention an FT article about model market share, not carded as harness material.
Whiteboard images and session code folders were not read; only transcript, README and meta file listed. meta.md files were not opened separately beyond README (not provided as content).
